summary: Daniel reads Jeremiah’s words about Jerusalem’s desolations and responds with fasting, confession, and petition. His prayer admits Israel’s disobedience, appeals to God’s mercy, and asks for Jerusalem and the sanctuary to be restored. While he is still praying, Gabriel comes to give him understanding about “seventy weeks,” a troubled rebuilding, an Anointed One, destruction, covenant, and desolation.
whyItMatters: This chapter joins Daniel’s prayerful response to exile with one of the book’s most debated visions of timed suffering and restoration. It shows Daniel seeking understanding from earlier prophetic words before receiving a new disclosure that remains difficult for readers to date and identify with certainty.

context.author: The visions speak in Daniel’s first-person voice, and this chapter is narrated by Daniel. The book does not name a final editor; traditional readers identify Daniel as author, while most critical scholarship sees a second-century BC final composition using older Daniel traditions.
context.audience: Jews pressured to surrender worship, practice, identity, or hope under imperial power, first narrated through exile and then addressed through apocalyptic vision.
context.date: The narrative setting is the first year of Darius over the Chaldeans. Most scholars date Daniel’s final Hebrew-Aramaic form to about 167–164 BC, while traditional readings place its authorship in the sixth century BC.
context.setting: The stories place Daniel in Babylonian and Persian-period courts after Jerusalem’s conquest and exile. Chapter 9 looks toward Jerusalem, its desolations, its sanctuary, and its future under troubled times.
context.literaryForm: Prayer of confession followed by apocalyptic revelation with angelic interpretation.

outline.heading: Daniel Reads Jeremiah
outline.note: The chapter opens in the first year of Darius, when Daniel understands from the books that Jeremiah’s word spoke of seventy years for Jerusalem’s desolations.

outline.heading: Daniel Seeks God
outline.note: Daniel turns to the Lord God with prayer, petitions, fasting, sackcloth, ashes, and begins by naming God’s covenant and loving kindness.

outline.heading: Confession of Israel’s Sin
outline.note: Daniel confesses collective rebellion, failure to listen to the prophets, and the justice of the calamity that has come on Jerusalem.

outline.heading: Petition for Jerusalem
outline.note: Daniel appeals to God’s past deliverance, mercy, name, city, holy mountain, and desolate sanctuary, asking God to hear, forgive, listen, and act.

outline.heading: Gabriel Arrives
outline.note: While Daniel is still confessing and praying, Gabriel comes, says Daniel is greatly beloved, and calls him to understand the vision.

outline.heading: Seventy Weeks Decreed
outline.note: Gabriel speaks of seventy weeks for Daniel’s people and holy city, including restoration, an Anointed One, destruction, covenant, ceased sacrifice, abominations, and a decreed end.

keyVerses.text: in the first year of his reign I, Daniel, understood by the books the number of the years about which Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah the prophet for the accomplishing of the desolations of Jerusalem, even seventy years.
keyVerses.why: This explains why Daniel prays: he is responding to a written prophetic word about Jerusalem’s desolations.

keyVerses.text: To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgiveness, for we have rebelled against him.
keyVerses.why: This line holds together the prayer’s two main claims: God’s mercy and the people’s rebellion.

keyVerses.text: My God, turn your ear and hear. Open your eyes and see our desolations, and the city which is called by your name; for we do not present our petitions before you for our righteousness, but for your great mercies’ sake.
keyVerses.why: Daniel grounds his request not in the people’s righteousness but in God’s mercy and in the city called by God’s name.

keyVerses.text: “Seventy weeks are decreed on your people and on your holy city, to finish disobedience, to make an end of sins, to make reconciliation for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most holy.
keyVerses.why: This begins Gabriel’s answer and introduces the chapter’s difficult timetable and its stated goals.

questions.question: Where does this chapter begin in Daniel’s story?
questions.answer: It begins in “the first year of Darius,” who is described as made king over the realm of the Chaldeans. The identification of Darius the Mede is historically difficult, so the safest orientation is to follow the chapter’s own setting without pretending the problem is settled.

questions.question: What does Daniel understand from “the books”?
questions.answer: Daniel understands that Yahweh’s word had come to Jeremiah about the desolations of Jerusalem lasting seventy years. The chapter says this reading leads into his prayer; it does not give all the details of Jeremiah’s prophecy inside Daniel 9 itself.

questions.question: Why does Daniel confess sins if he is asking for Jerusalem to be restored?
questions.answer: Daniel’s prayer treats the disaster as bound up with Israel’s failure to listen, obey, and turn back. He does not present the people as deserving restoration; he appeals to God’s mercies, God’s name, and the city and sanctuary that are desolate.

questions.question: What does “confusion of face” mean here?
questions.answer: In this chapter the phrase names public shame or disgrace. Daniel says righteousness belongs to God, while “confusion of face” belongs to Judah, Jerusalem, Israel, kings, princes, and fathers because they have sinned and trespassed.

questions.question: Does Daniel say God was unfair to Jerusalem?
questions.answer: No. Daniel repeatedly says God is righteous and that the evil brought on Jerusalem confirmed earlier words of warning. That does not make the suffering small, but the prayer frames it as the result of covenant disobedience rather than as injustice by God.

questions.question: What is Daniel asking God to do in verses 16-19?
questions.answer: He asks God to turn anger away from Jerusalem, listen to his prayer, make God’s face shine on the desolate sanctuary, see the desolations, forgive, and act without delay. His reasons are God’s righteousness, God’s mercies, and God’s own name attached to the city and people.

questions.question: Who is Gabriel in this chapter?
questions.answer: The chapter calls Gabriel “the man Gabriel” and identifies him as the one Daniel had seen in an earlier vision. Here he comes while Daniel is praying and says he has come to give Daniel wisdom and understanding.

questions.question: What are the “seventy weeks”?
questions.answer: Gabriel says seventy weeks are decreed on Daniel’s people and holy city, but the chapter does not supply a single agreed modern calendar conversion. Readers differ over starting points and identifications; the clearer claim is that the period is bounded and directed toward ending disobedience, dealing with sin, righteousness, vision, prophecy, and the most holy.

questions.question: Who is the “Anointed One” in verses 25-26?
questions.answer: The chapter says an Anointed One, the prince, comes after seven weeks and sixty-two weeks, and that after the sixty-two weeks the Anointed One will be cut off and have nothing. Readers differ: Jewish and critical readings often connect the language to figures and events around Jerusalem’s restoration or later persecution, while Christian readings often connect it to Christ. The chapter itself gives the title and sequence but does not name the figure in a way that removes all debate.

glossary.def: The ruler named at the start of the chapter, described as the son of Ahasuerus and as made king over the realm of the Chaldeans.
The ruined condition associated with Jerusalem in this chapter; Daniel reads about Jerusalem’s desolations and later asks God to see “our desolations.”
Signs of mourning or humbled petition that accompany Daniel’s prayer and fasting in verse 3.
The heavenly messenger who comes to Daniel during prayer and says he has come to give wisdom and understanding.
The period Gabriel says is decreed for Daniel’s people and holy city; its exact calculation and fulfillment are debated by readers.
